## Abstract

Feedback linearization is a powerful tool in nonlinear control, but finding the linearizing coordinate transform remains challenging. Feedback linearizing transforms are governed by well-established partial differential equations (PDEs) whose well-posedness is based on the Lie-algebraic Frobenius theorem, but solving the PDEs becomes computationally intractable for large system dimensions. To address this challenge, we propose a cascaded physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework to approximately solve these PDEs. By separately parameterizing terms of different Lie derivative orders, we mitigate the compounding errors inherent in fitting high-order Lie derivatives of neural networks. Furthermore, we use the learned transform to design a tracking controller and establish theoretical bounds on its error with respect to inaccuracies in the learned feedback-linearizing representation. We validate our method on a broad class of feedback linearizable systems, including a multi-input, multi-output planar quadrotor and synthetic examples for which analytical approaches are impractical, and demonstrate that our approach can computationally discover effective feedback-linearizing representations of nonlinear systems for control tasks.

## I Introduction

Feedback linearization transforms nonlinear dynamics into an equivalent linear system via feedback transformation [9]. Once found, this transform enables the application of powerful tools from linear systems theory to control complex, nonlinear systems. The existence of such transforms depends on a Lie-algebraic Frobenius condition; when the Frobenius condition holds, there exists a well-posed system of partial differential equations (PDEs) whose solution and associated Lie derivatives provide the linearizing coordinates. However, solving the PDEs is challenging in general. Analytical approaches are customized and highly system-specific, while algorithmic approaches are scarce and suffer from significant computational shortcomings [20].

Recently, PINNs [17] have emerged as an efficient method to approximate PDE solutions with applications to, for example, optimal control [5] and reachability [2]. PINNs recast PDE solutions as minimizers of a residual loss. As such, their computational cost empirically scales with solution complexity rather than grid resolution [2], improving performance on higher-dimensional problems.

We leverage the computational benefits of PINNs to systematically discover feedback-linearizing representations of nonlinear systems. Two key technical challenges arise. First, during learning, the high-order Lie derivatives in the governing PDEs introduce computational bottlenecks and compounding approximation errors. To overcome this, we introduce a cascaded neural network structure that decomposes complex, high-order PDEs into a sequence of tractable, first-order residual minimizations. We demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms naive PINN baselines and accurately reconstructs linearizing behavior. Second, controller design must account for the effects of a learned (approximate) representation on downstream control performance. We design a controller using the learned transform and bound its downstream tracking error with respect to learning errors. Evaluated on both physical and synthetic systems up to eight dimensions, our work constitutes the first systematic application of PINNs for discovering feedback linearizing representations.

### I-A Related Work

#### I-A1 Learning Linear Representations of Nonlinear Systems

Prior learning-based approaches for feedback linearization focus primarily on compensating for uncertain dynamics when the linearizing outputs are already known, whether by directly approximating the linearizing control law [25, 18, 21, 24] or modeling the dynamic mismatch from an imperfect linearization [8, 7]. In contrast, we consider the inverse problem of discovering linearizing outputs when the dynamics are perfectly known. Separately, Goswami et al. [6] aims to discover linearizing transforms via purely data-driven invertible neural networks, which limits downstream control analysis. By contrast, our approach is model-based, solving the governing PDE conditions to discover the desired linear representation while enabling formal tracking error bounds. Other linearizing frameworks, such as Koopman operator approaches [4, 13, 15], focus largely on system dynamics and do not leverage control-oriented structure like the Frobenius condition.

#### I-A2 Physics-Informed Neural Networks in Control

By casting PDE solving as optimization over sampled points, PINNs [17] have been successfully applied to control tasks involving Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman [5] and Hamilton-Jacobi-reachability equations [2]. However, their application to feedback linearization remains unexplored. A primary barrier is that naively applying PINNs to the high-order PDEs that characterize linearizing transforms introduces significant computational bottlenecks and numerical inaccuracies—challenges we overcome in this work through a novel cascadic training algorithm.

### I-B Statement of Contributions

Our contributions are threefold. We present:

- • A novel, cascaded physics-informed learning method that efficiently approximates linearizing transforms for both single-input single-output (SISO) and multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems;

- • A realizable controller with learning-aware tracking error bounds that depend explicitly on the quality of the learned coordinate transform, directly linking the learning effectiveness to control performance;

- • Extensive empirical validation demonstrating our method’s capacity to effectively feedback-linearize a broad class of complex dynamical systems, including a planar quadrotor model and systems for which analytical solutions are intractable.

### I-C Notations

We use $D_{\mathbf{x}}f$ to denote the derivative of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ . When $f$ and $\mathbf{x}$ are both vectors, $D_{\mathbf{x}}f$ denotes the Jacobian. We use the notation $\mathcal{L}_{f}h(\mathbf{x}):=D_{\mathbf{x}}h(\mathbf{x})\cdot f(\mathbf{x})$ to denote the Lie derivative of $h$ along the vector field $f$ . We use $\mathrm{ad}_{f}g:=[f,g]=D_{\mathbf{x}}g\cdot f-D_{\mathbf{x}}f\cdot g$ to denote the Lie bracket between vector fields $f$ and $g$ . For convenience, we denote the iterative Lie brackets as $\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{k+1}g:=[f,\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{k}g]$ with $\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{0}g=g$ .

## II Problem Formulation

Consider the nonlinear, MIMO, control-affine system

$$ \dot{\mathbf{x}}=f(\mathbf{x})+g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}, $$

where state $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , input $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ , and $f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n},g:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ are smooth vector fields. Given perfect knowledge of $f$ and $g$ over an open region $\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , our objective is to learn a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a nonlinear feedback control law $\mathbf{u}=\psi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})$ such that the transformed state $\mathbf{z}=\Phi(\mathbf{x})$ follows linear, time-invariant dynamics

$$ \dot{\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v}, $$

where $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})$ is a canonical Brunovsky pair (i.e. a decoupled chain of integrators). Henceforth, we assume that such a diffeomorphism $\Phi(\mathbf{x})$ exists and refer to it as the linearizing coordinate transform.

The paper is organized as follows: PDE conditions for feedback linearization are posed in Section III, motivating a physics-informed learning framework developed in Section IV. Section V bounds the effects of learning error on downstream tracking performance; Section VI presents extensive experimental validation of our approach.

## III Background on Feedback Linearization

The theory of feedback linearization yields a set of PDEs whose solution directly determines the linearizing coordinate transform $\Phi$ . For clarity, we restrict our exposition to the SISO case ( $m=1$ ); the MIMO generalization is presented in the Appendix -A of the full version [11]. For SISO systems, existence of a linearizing coordinate transform is equivalent to that of a smooth, real-valued linearizing output $h(\mathbf{x})$ with relative degree $n$ on the domain $\mathcal{D}$ (see Lemma 4.2.1 in [9]). Thus, for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}$ , $h(\mathbf{x})$ satisfies:

- CA1 $\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{i}h(\mathbf{x})=0$ for $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-2\}$ ,

- CA2 $\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{n-1}h(\mathbf{x})\neq 0$ .

The linearizing transform is constructed by direct concatenation of $h(\mathbf{x})$ and its Lie derivatives. Concretely: $\Phi(\mathbf{x})=[\Phi_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\dots,\Phi_{n}(\mathbf{x})]^{\top}$ , where

$$ \Phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{L}^{i-1}_{f}h(\mathbf{x}). $$

The corresponding linearizing control law is given as

$$ \mathbf{u}=\psi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})=A_{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})^{-1}(\mathbf{v}-b_{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})), $$

where $A_{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})={\mathcal{L}_{g}\Phi_{n}(\mathbf{x})}$ and $b_{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{L}_{f}\Phi_{n}(\mathbf{x})$ . CA readily defines a set of PDE conditions on $h(\mathbf{x})$ whose solution fully parameterizes the desired transform $\Phi$ via (3). However, learning this solution is challenging due to the presence of high-order Lie derivatives. To reduce the order, the Lie derivatives are recast in terms of iterated Lie brackets to get the following set of equivalent, first-order conditions:

- CB1 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{i}g}h(\mathbf{x})=0$ for $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-2\}$ ,

- CB2 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g}h(\mathbf{x})=(-1)^{n-1}\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{n-1}h\neq 0$ .

While (CB1) constitutes a set of $n-1$ equalities

$$ D_{\mathbf{x}}h\cdot\begin{bmatrix}g&\mathrm{ad}_{f}g&\ldots&\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-2}g\end{bmatrix}=0 $$

that are well-suited to regression (see Section IV), the non-triviality condition (CB2) ensuring the numerical stability of the control law (4) is underconstrained. One approach, consistent with (CB1), is to enforce

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g}h(\mathbf{x})=c $$

for a nonzero constant $c$ over the domain $\mathcal{D}$ . However, this equality formulation is restrictive; a solution can fail to exist for (6) even when one exists for CB. In Section IV we propose a more general method to reformulate this condition. Concluding the theoretical background, we note that our method also applies naturally to the MIMO setting, deferring further details to Appendix -A.

## IV Learning Linearizing Transformations

We propose a PINN framework to compute the desired diffeomorphism $\Phi$ by approximating solutions to the linearizing PDE conditions. We first present a direct Lie bracket-based algorithm for learning the linearizing output, and show that constructing the diffeomorphism through high-order differentiation of this output introduces severe compounding errors. We then introduce a novel cascaded neural network structure that sequentially minimizes tractable, first-order residuals to mitigate these errors and enable effective downstream control.

### IV-A Learning Linearizing Outputs

PINNs [17] compute approximate PDE solutions by parameterizing the candidate function as a deep neural network and minimizing the PDE residuals via a standard loss function. Defining the candidate linearizing output $h_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$ with network weights $\theta$ , the consequent PDE residuals of (CB1) are compactly expressed as

$$ \mathcal{RB}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}):=D_{\mathbf{x}}h_{\theta}\cdot\begin{bmatrix}g&\mathrm{ad}_{f}g&\ldots&\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-2}g\end{bmatrix}, $$

while the non-triviality residual of (CB2) is expressed as

$$ \mathcal{SB}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}):=D_{\mathbf{x}}h_{\theta}\cdot\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g. $$

We appeal to the first-order Lie bracket-based conditions CB, to circumvent the computational complexity introduced by the high order Lie derivatives in CA. Since $\mathcal{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is compact and $\mathcal{SB}(\mathbf{x})=D_{\mathbf{x}}h\cdot\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g$ is continuous for any continuously differentiable $h(\mathbf{x})$ , we can always pick $a,b>0$ as hyperparameters and find a linearizing output s.t. $\mathcal{SB}(\mathbf{x})\in[a,b]$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}$ , ensuring non-triviality while preserving regularity (e.g., to avoid excessively large control gains). We can now train the network $h_{\theta}(x)$ to approximate such an output using the composite loss

$$ L(\theta)=L_{\mathcal{RB}}(\theta)+L_{\mathcal{SB}}(\theta), $$

with $L_{\mathcal{RB}}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}||\mathcal{RB}_{\theta}(x_{i})||^{2}_{2}$ to enforce the desired bracket annihilation and $L_{\mathcal{SB}}(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\max(a-\mathcal{SB}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i}),0)+\max(\mathcal{SB}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-b,0))^{2}$ to impose the box constraints preventing triviality.

### IV-B Difficulty in Constructing $\Phi$ via Differentiation

While the loss function (7) serves as an effective supervision for finding linearizing outputs, constructing the diffeomorphism $\Phi$ requires the complete set of Lie derivatives that appear in CA. However, we observe that a neural network trained under loss (7) can only approximate a true linearizing output well up to its first derivative – the highest order derivative that is explicitly supervised. This limitation is closely related to the deep learning phenomenon of spectral bias [16], which describes the tendency of neural networks to preferentially approximate low-frequency components of a target function. This bias is detrimental to the approximation of higher order Lie derivatives, since differentiation amplifies errors proportionally to frequency.

Additionally, the small first-order bracket errors (7) in the learned outputs can be amplified via high-order differentiation, as illustrated in the following lemma.

#### Lemma 1.

Let $e_{i}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{i}g}h(\mathbf{x})$ , for $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}$ , be the residuals of (CA1). We also define the residuals in (CB1) as $\epsilon_{i}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{i}h(\mathbf{x})$ . Assuming known $e_{i}$ for $i\in\{0,\ldots,k\}$ , $\epsilon_{i}$ is computed with the iterative formula:

$$ \epsilon_{i}=(-1)^{i}e_{i}+\sum_{r=0}^{i-1}(-1)^{r+i+1}\binom{i}{r}\mathcal{L}_{f}\epsilon_{r}. $$

A direct consequence of Lemma 4.1.2 in [9], this result formalizes the attenuation of implicit supervision over (CA1) residuals $e_{i}$ when training on (CB1), as the minimization targets $\epsilon_{i}$ come to be dominated by the accumulating right-most terms. Thus, the direct approach only weakly penalizes violations of higher-order Lie derivative conditions, compromising the reliability of the learned transform in downstream control tasks.

To mitigate this, one could augment the loss in (7) with explicit supervision of higher order Lie derivatives via the conditions CA. However, incorporating high-order Lie derivatives introduces significant computational and optimization challenges. Although the former can be addressed to some extent by Taylor-mode automatic differentiation [3], the latter make this approach impractical as system complexity grows (see Section VI).

### IV-C Cascadic Learning of the Diffeomorphism

To overcome the limitations of direct bracket-based supervision, we adopt a cascaded representation using separate neural networks

$$ \hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x}):=\begin{pmatrix}h_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,h_{\theta_{n}}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix}, $$

parametrizing the linearizing coordinate transform $\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\Phi}_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,\hat{\Phi}_{n}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix}$ . Exploiting the ability of the bracket-based approach to approximate a linearizing output up to its first order, we combine this cascaded structure with a curriculum training strategy. In particular, we first train $h_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x})$ using (7). Then, for $i=2,\dots,n$ , we train each $h_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x})$ in succession by minimizing

$$ L(\theta_{i})=L_{\mathcal{F}}(\theta_{i})+L_{\mathcal{G}}(\theta_{i}), $$

where the consistency term

$$ L_{\mathcal{F}}(\theta_{i})=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{f}h_{\theta_{i-1}}(\mathbf{x}_{j})-h_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x}_{j})\bigr)^{2} $$

encourages reconstruction of the Lie derivative of the preceding layer $h_{\theta_{i-1}}$ , while the control-specific term

$$ L_{\mathcal{G}}(\theta_{i})=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\bigl(\mathcal{L}_{g}h_{\theta_{i}}(\mathbf{x}_{j})\bigr)^{2} $$

promotes adherence to conditions CA.

Intuitively, the cascadic approach decomposes the original learning problem—where a single network must satisfy conditions involving Lie derivatives up to order $n$ —into a sequence of simpler tasks involving only first-order derivatives across multiple networks. By relaxing the implicit constraint that $\hat{\Phi}_{i+1}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\Phi}_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ , the resulting coordinate transform satisfies CA more tightly than approaches relying solely on bracket-based supervision. Moreover, this formulation avoids the optimization pathologies associated with explicitly supervising high-order Lie derivatives. Empirically, the cascadic approach demonstrates superior performance and reliability compared to single-network formulations.

```


1: Input: Training set $\{\mathbf{x}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$

2: Output: Learned transform $\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})=\bigl(h_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,h_{\theta_{n}}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)$

3: Initialize $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}$

4: Train $h_{\theta_{1}}$ according to (7)
5: Freeze $h_{\theta_{1}}$

6: for $i=2,\ldots,n$ do
7: Train $h_{\theta_{i}}$ according to (9)
8: Freeze $h_{\theta_{i}}$
9: end for

10: return $\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})=\bigl(h_{\theta_{1}}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,h_{\theta_{n}}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)$

```

We conclude with a brief remark on computational complexity. The cascadic approach requires only first-order derivatives for training, significantly reducing the computational cost of constructing high-order derivatives as compared to direct approaches while yielding linear scaling with the number of cascade stages. Further, in MIMO settings only the decoupling matrix requires joint training, and the remaining layers can be trained independently to admit straightforward parallelization.

## V Tracking Control with Learned Coordinate Transform

To illustrate how learning errors manifest in downstream control performance, we consider the task of following a dynamically feasible and bounded reference trajectory $(\bar{\mathbf{x}},\bar{\mathbf{u}})$ under the nonlinear dynamics (1). With the learned, approximately linearizing, transform $\hat{\Phi}$ , we design an error-feedback controller in the linearized space. We characterize the tracking error of this controller in terms of learning losses. Before proceeding, we make the following assumptions on the map $\hat{\Phi}$ .11 1 Empirically, we observe no invertibility issues in the examples considered. We further analyze in the Appendix how training errors affect the invertibility of the learned transform relative to the assumed ground-truth linearizing diffeomorphism.

#### Assumption 1.

$\hat{\Phi}$ is invertible. Further, there exists a positive constant $l_{\hat{\Phi}}$ such that $l_{\hat{\Phi}}\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{2}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x}_{1})-\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x}_{2})\right\rVert$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}$ .

The invertibility of $\hat{\Phi}$ is necessary to relate the tracking error in the linearized domain to that in the nonlinear domain and is a standard assumption for analyzing approximate linearizing transforms [10]. The existence of $l_{\hat{\Phi}}$ ensures that the inverse is not arbitrarily ill-conditioned.

Let $\bar{\mathbf{z}}=\hat{\Phi}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})$ be the reference linearized state and $\bar{\mathbf{v}}:=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\Phi}_{n-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})+\mathcal{L}_{g}\hat{\Phi}_{n-1}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\bar{\mathbf{u}}$ as the reference virtual input. We define the control law in the linearized space:

$$ \mathbf{v}(t)=\bar{\mathbf{v}}(t)-\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{z}-\bar{\mathbf{z}}(t)), $$

where $\mathbf{K}$ is a robust stabilizing gain matrix designed by solving the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ Riccati equation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{P}\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{P}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{P}=-\mathbf{Q}-\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}. $$

Here, $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})$ is the Brunovsky pair, and $\mathbf{Q}$ , $\mathbf{R}$ are properly chosen cost matrices. The gain matrix is then taken to be $\mathbf{K}=\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{P}$ . Applying the linearizing control law (4), the control input is given as

$$ \mathbf{u}=A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})\left(\bar{v}-\mathbf{K}\left(\mathbf{z}-\bar{\mathbf{z}}\right)-b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})\right). $$

Because of the existence of learning errors, $\hat{\Phi}$ does not perfectly linearize the $\mathbf{z}$ -space dynamics and leads to the perturbed $\mathbf{z}$ -dynamics

$$ \dot{\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+(\mathbf{B}+\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x}))\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{d}_{z}(\mathbf{x}), $$

where the multiplicative input disturbance $\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x})$ and the drift $\mathbf{d}_{z}(\mathbf{x})$ arise from $\hat{\Phi}$ not perfectly satisfying conditions CA. Two sources of learning inaccuracy drive these terms: the PDE residuals $r_{i}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathcal{L}_{g}\hat{\Phi}_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ , and the cascade consistency errors $\mathbf{d}_{c}(\mathbf{x})$ , with $i$ -th element $\mathbf{d}_{c,i}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\Phi}_{i-1}(\mathbf{x})-\hat{\Phi}_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ . Denoting the stacked residual ${\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{x}):=[r_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\cdots,r_{n-2}(\mathbf{x}),0]}$ , the perturbation terms can be expressed as

$$ \begin{gathered}\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{x})A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}),\\
\mathbf{d}_{z}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{x})A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{d}_{c}(\mathbf{x}).\end{gathered} $$

Note that the PDE residuals $\mathbf{r}$ and consistency error $\mathbf{d}_{c}$ are explicitly minimized during training via corresponding loss terms in (9). Further, given that $A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible (promoted via the term $L_{\mathcal{S}}$ in (7)), $\left\lVert\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_{F}$ and $\left\lVert\mathbf{d}_{z}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_{2}$ vanish as $\mathbf{r}$ and $\mathbf{d}_{c}$ approach zero. Thus, when the learning error is small, it is reasonable to assume that the disturbance terms (15) are small and bounded over the training domain.

#### Assumption 2.

We assume that for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{D}$ , the disturbance terms $\left\lVert\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_{F}\leq\bar{\delta},\;\left\lVert\mathbf{d}_{z}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\bar{d}.$

Finally, to ensure safety, the reference trajectory must maintain a sufficient margin strictly within the domain where our learning guarantees hold.

#### Assumption 3.

The reference virtual input is bounded by $\|\bar{\mathbf{v}}(t)\|\leq\bar{V}$ , and the reference states $\mathbf{x}(t)$ remain strictly inside the interior of the training domain $\mathcal{D}$ .

In the interest of space, we present an informal version of the result, deferring the formal statement and proof to Appendix -B of the full version [11].

#### Theorem 2 (informal).

Suppose Assumptions 1–3 hold and that the input perturbation is sufficiently small such that $\bar{\delta}<\sqrt{\lambda_{\text{min}}(\mathbf{R})}/\gamma$ . Then, there exists a forward-invariant set $\Omega_{x}=\{\mathbf{e}\mid\left\lVert\mathbf{e}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq r_{\mathbf{e}}^{2}\}$ for the state tracking error $\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ . The radius $r_{\mathbf{e}}$ is bounded by the additive and multiplicative learning errors and scales as:

$$ r_{\mathbf{e}}^{2}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{{\bar{d}}^{2}+\bar{\delta}^{2}\bar{V}^{2}}{\lambda_{\text{min}}(\mathbf{R})-\gamma^{2}{\bar{\delta}}^{2}}\right). $$

Consequently, if the initial state satisfies $\mathbf{e}_{x}(0)\in\Omega_{x}$ , and the reference trajectory maintains a safety margin from the boundary of $\mathcal{D}$ such that $\bar{\mathbf{x}}(t)\in\mathcal{D}\ominus\Omega_{x}$ , the true state $\mathbf{x}(t)$ never leaves $\mathcal{D}$ , guaranteeing that the local error bounds hold for all $t\geq 0$ .

Theorem 2 formalizes the relationship between the learning errors and closed-loop control. Driving the PDE residuals $\mathbf{r}(x)$ and consistency errors $\mathbf{d}_{c}(\mathbf{x})$ to zero during training directly shrinks $\bar{\delta}$ and $\bar{d}$ , thereby tightening the guarantees on downstream tracking performance. In Section VI, we approximate these worst-case bounds by densely sampling the training domain and taking the maximum observed values of $\delta(\mathbf{x})$ and $d(\mathbf{x})$ . Extending PINN generalization analyses such as [14] to obtain certified bounds between samples is an important direction of future work.

## VI Experiments

We test our learning algorithm and the corresponding learned downstream controllers in an extensive array of feedback linearizable systems. We first test our method on well-known examples that admit analytic linearizing output solutions; these instances have simple (e.g., affine) forms that are easy to learn. Then, to further stress-test our approach, we synthesize complex SISO and MIMO systems for which analytical solutions are intractable. The results show that our approach can achieve good empirical performance for systems of various sizes in terms of both the quality of the linearizing transform and the controller performance.

### VI-A Learning Setup and Evaluation

We employ Jaxpi [22] as our PINN implementation framework and adopt the modified MLP architecture proposed in [23] for our candidate PDE solutions, as it exhibits superior performance compared to standard feed-forward MLPs. As a baseline, we implement the direct single-network approach that learns a linearizing output supervised by both conditions CA and CB.

In addition to reporting the metrics explicitly included in the losses supervising training, we seek to directly measure how well the learned coordinate transform linearizes the system dynamics. To do so, we sample $\mathbf{x}$ uniformly in $\mathcal{D}$ , $\mathbf{u}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bf{0},\mathbf{I})$ and compute the difference between the true time derivative of the transform $\dot{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})=D_{\mathbf{x}}\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})(f(\mathbf{x})+g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u})$ and the time derivative predicted by the linear dynamics $\dot{\hat{\Phi}}^{pred}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{A}\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\Phi}_{n-1}(\mathbf{x})+\mathcal{L}_{g}\hat{\Phi}_{n-1}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u})$ . We then measure the quality of linearization as the relative error of the true and approximate time derivatives:

$$ \varepsilon(\mathbf{x}):=\left\lVert\dot{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})-\dot{\hat{\Phi}}^{pred}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert{\big/}\left\lVert\dot{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})\right\rVert. $$

This relative linearization quality error (RLQE) is especially useful for comparing our proposed cascadic approach and the single network baseline, as the former intentionally introduces a cascade inconsistency between $T_{i+1}(\mathbf{x})$ and $\mathcal{L}_{f}T_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ but the latter does not, making their PDE residual not directly comparable. In contrast, RLQE provides a fair comparison as it directly quantifies the quality of the downstream linearization. Finally, we report the folded fraction: the proportion of sampled states at which the sign of $det(D_{\mathbf{x}}\Phi)$ differs from the dominant sign of the rest of the samples, implying that the learned transform ceases to be a diffeomorphism.

### VI-B Controller Setup and Evaluation

Once the linearizing coordinate transform is learned, we construct the downstream tracking controller following the procedure in Section V with $\mathbf{Q}:=q\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{R}:=\mathbf{I}$ , where $q\in[1,5]$ is system-specific. To evaluate the controller, we generate 64 reference trajectories for each system by using a ground-truth feedback linearization controller to regulate the state to the origin from initial conditions randomly sampled from the interior of the domain. Example reference trajectories are visualized in Figures 1 and 2. To test robustness, we apply the tracking controller from perturbed initial conditions, with perturbations sampled from an $\ell_{\infty}$ ball of radius $0.15$ . We simulate the controllers for $T\in[8,10]$ seconds with RK45 numerical integration and a step size of $0.002$ s.

We evaluate the tracking controller with the average tracking error ( $\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\left\lVert\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert\mathrm{d}t$ ), the final state error ( $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}(T)-\bar{\mathbf{x}}(T)\right\rVert$ ), and the total control effort ( $\int_{0}^{T}\left\lVert\mathbf{u}\right\rVert\mathrm{d}t$ ). For each system, we report the median errors among the 64 reference trajectories, along with the number of diverging trajectories, to capture potential stability issues. To contextualize the results, we also report the performance of a feedback linearization controller constructed with the ground-truth diffeomorphism.

#### VI-D2 4D SISO Systems

We now compare the direct and cascadic methods on 4D SISO systems. Across 10 randomly generated systems, the cascadic approach achieves an RLQE two orders of magnitude lower than the direct method and prevents the severe folding observed in the latter, effectively mitigating problems arising from high-order derivatives supervision. Furthermore, we empirically observe that the quasi-singularities of $D_{\mathbf{x}}\Phi$ are highly correlated with large evaluation errors of the supervision losses across all methods and systems. Finally, our cascadic approach is consistently stable and matches the tracking performance of the ground-truth controller. In contrast, the direct approach diverges on half of the tested systems (29 out of 640 trajectories across 10 systems). These results establish that a cascaded structure is critical for applying PINN-based methods to complex nonlinear systems.

#### VI-D3 8D MIMO Systems

Finally, we evaluate the generalization of both approaches to MIMO systems by considering 8D MIMO systems with two fourth-degree linearizing outputs. The increased system dimension, together with the need to learn multiple outputs, introduces additional challenges for the proposed method. However, the learned coordinate transforms again achieve tracking performance on par with the ground-truth controller. Comparing the two learning approaches, we should also emphasize that the direct approach is not only more computationally inefficient in this setting, but also yields a more fragile approximation of the diffeomorphism. Concretely, the significant empirical folded fraction implies an ill-conditioned representation, undermining the reliability of the downstream controller.

## VII Conclusion

This paper introduced a cascadic physics-informed neural network method to systematically discover feedback-linearizing coordinate transforms for nonlinear systems. By decomposing complex, high-order partial differential equations into a sequence of tractable, first-order residual minimizations, our approach successfully mitigated compounding approximation errors and enabled robust downstream tracking control. Extensive validation demonstrated strong empirical performance across real robotic systems and complex synthetic systems of up to eight dimensions. Future work will extend this framework to approximately linearizable systems ([12, 10]), systems with non-trivial zero-dynamics, and to systems where the underlying dynamics are subject to uncertainty.

### -A FBL for Multi-Input Multi-Output Systems

Similar to the SISO setting presented in Section III, the conditions for exact feedback linearization of the control affine system (1) in the MIMO setting mirrors can be characterized in terms of the relative degree of the system. Recall that a function $h(x)$ has relative degree $r$ , when, for all $x\in\mathcal{D}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{g_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{i}h(\mathbf{x})=0\quad\forall i\in\{0,\ldots,r-2\},j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{g_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r-1}h(\mathbf{x})\neq 0\quad\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}. $$

Consider a set of real-valued smooth functions $\{h_{i}(x)\}_{i=1}^{m}$ , each with relative degree $r_{i}$ . Denoting $\mathbf{z}_{i}=h_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ , we have that the linearized state $\mathbf{z}:=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{m}\end{pmatrix}$ evolves as $m$ decoupled chains of integrators (i.e. in Brunovsky canonical form). Specifically, denoting the $r$ -th time derivative of $z_{i}$ as $h^{(r)}$ , we get:

$$ \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{z}_{1}^{(r_{1})},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(r_{m})}\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{v}:=b(\mathbf{x})+A(\mathbf{x})u, $$

where the drift term $b:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}$ and the decoupling matrix $A:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ can be written down analytically, respectively as

$$ \displaystyle A(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{g_{1}}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{1}-1}h_{1}(\mathbf{x})&\ldots&\mathcal{L}_{g_{m}}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{1}-1}h_{1}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\mathcal{L}_{g_{1}}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{m}-1}h_{m}(\mathbf{x})&\ldots&\mathcal{L}_{g_{m}}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{m}-1}h_{m}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix}, $$

$$ b(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{1}}h_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{m}}h_{m}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix}. $$

Denote the map $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}$ as:

$$ \Phi(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}h_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{1}-1}h_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,h_{m}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,\mathcal{L}_{f}^{r_{m}-1}h_{m}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix}. $$

When the decoupling matrix $A(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible and the total relative degree of the system $r:=r_{1}+\ldots+r_{m}$ matches the state dimension $n$ , i.e.,

$$ r_{1}+\ldots+r_{m}=n, $$

the map $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism and a linearizing coordinate transform for the system (1). The corresponding linearizing control law is given as

$$ \mathbf{u}=A(\mathbf{x})^{-1}(\mathbf{v}-b(\mathbf{x})), $$

which is equivalent to the SISO case.

### -B Proof of Theorem 2 in the General MIMO setting

We prove Theorem 2 in the MIMO setting, which implies the results in Section V as special cases. Similar to the SISO setting, we consider the task of following a feasible trajectory $(\bar{\mathbf{x}},\bar{\mathbf{u}})$ and assume that the reference trajectory lies within the training domain.

#### Assumption 4.

Recall that the linearizing coordinate transform takes the form of (22). Therefore, we denote our in learned, approximate diffeomorphism $\hat{\Phi}$ as

$$ \mathbf{z}=\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})=\Big(\hat{\Phi}_{1,1}(\mathbf{x}),\cdots,\hat{\Phi}_{1,r_{1}}(\mathbf{x}),\cdots,\hat{\Phi}_{m,1}(\mathbf{x}),\cdots,\hat{\Phi}_{m,r_{m}}(\mathbf{x})\Big)^{\top}. $$

Mirroring the expressions in (20) and (21), we define

$$ A_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{g_{1}}\hat{\Phi}_{1,r_{1}}(\mathbf{x})&\ldots&\mathcal{L}_{g_{m}}\hat{\Phi}_{1,r_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\mathcal{L}_{g_{1}}\hat{\Phi}_{m,r_{m}}(\mathbf{x})&\ldots&\mathcal{L}_{g_{m}}\hat{\Phi}_{m,r_{m}}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix},\quad b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\Phi}_{1,r_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\\
\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\Phi}_{m,r_{m}}(\mathbf{x})\end{pmatrix}. $$

The error-feedback control law takes the same form as in the SISO setting:

$$ \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t)=-A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})\left(b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})-(\bar{\mathbf{v}}(t)+\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{z}-\bar{\mathbf{z}}(t))\right). $$

Here, $\bar{\mathbf{z}}:=\hat{\Phi}(\mathbf{x})$ , $\bar{\mathbf{v}}:=A_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})u+b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})$ , and the robust feedback gain $\mathbf{K}$ is found by solving the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ Riccati equation (12) with appropriate choices of $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ .

To start, we note that under the coordinate transform $\hat{\Phi}$ , the approximately linearized $\mathbf{z}$ dynamics follows

$$ \dot{\mathbf{z}}=\frac{d}{dt}\hat{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{d}{dt}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\\
\frac{d}{dt}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,r_{1}-1}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{f}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\\
\mathcal{L}_{f}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,r_{1}-1}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{L}_{g_{i}}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}_{i}\\
\vdots\\
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{L}_{g_{i}}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,r_{1}-1}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}_{i}\\
\vdots\end{bmatrix}. $$

To streamline notation, we define the vector function $\mathbf{d}^{c}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and matrix function $\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ as

$$ \mathbf{d}^{c}(\mathbf{x}):=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{L}_{f}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})-{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,2}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\\
\mathcal{L}_{f}{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,r_{1}-1}(\mathbf{x})-{\hat{\Phi}}_{1,r_{1}}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\end{bmatrix},\quad[\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x})]_{i,j}=\mathcal{L}_{g_{j}}{\hat{\Phi}}_{i}(\mathbf{x}). $$

Applying the control (25), the $\mathbf{z}$ dynamics (26) evolves as

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\mathbf{z}} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{d}^{c}(\mathbf{x})\right)+\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{d}^{c}(\mathbf{x})\right)+\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x})A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})\left(\mathbf{v}-b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})\right) \displaystyle=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}+\left(\mathbf{B}+\underbrace{\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x})A^{-1}(\mathbf{x})}_{=:\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x})}\right)\mathbf{v}+\left(\underbrace{\mathbf{d}^{c}(\mathbf{x})-\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x})A_{\hat{\Phi}}^{-1}(\mathbf{x})b_{\hat{\Phi}}(\mathbf{x})}_{=:\mathbf{d}^{z}(\mathbf{x})}\right). $$

Define the $\mathbf{z}$ -state error as $\mathbf{e}:=\mathbf{z}-\bar{\mathbf{z}}$ . The error dynamics evolve as

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\mathbf{e}} \displaystyle=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}+(\mathbf{B}+\mathbf{\Delta}_{B}(\mathbf{x}))\mathbf{K}\mathbf{e}+\underbrace{(\mathbf{\Delta}_{B}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{\Delta}_{B}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}))\bar{\mathbf{v}}+\mathbf{d}^{z}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{d}^{z}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})}_{=:\mathbf{d}}. $$

We assume that the error terms $\Delta_{B}$ and $\mathbf{d}^{z}$ are small when the models are well-trained on the domain.

#### Assumption 5.

Note that from Assumption 5, we clearly have that

$$ \left\lVert\mathbf{d}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\Delta_{B}(\mathbf{x})+\Delta_{B}(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\right\rVert\left\lVert\bar{\mathbf{v}}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\mathbf{d}^{z}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{d}^{z}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})\right\rVert\leq 2(\bar{\delta}\bar{V}+\bar{d}^{z})=:\bar{d}. $$

The boundedness of the approximation errors and the reference signal allows us to establish a forward-invariant set of the $\mathbf{z}$ tracking error.

$$ \displaystyle\dot{V}(\mathbf{e}) \displaystyle\leq-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{e}-\frac{1}{2}\eta\left\lVert\mathbf{P}\mathbf{e}\right\rVert^{2}+\bar{d}\left\lVert\mathbf{P}\mathbf{e}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{e}^{\top}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{e}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt{\eta}\left\lVert\mathbf{P}\mathbf{e}\right\rVert-\frac{\bar{d}}{\sqrt{\eta}}\right)^{2}+\frac{\bar{d}^{2}}{2\eta} \displaystyle\leq-\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{\text{min}}(\mathbf{Q})\left\lVert\mathbf{e}\right\rVert^{2}+\frac{\bar{d}^{2}}{2\eta} $$

As a result, the Lyapunov function is strictly decreasing when $\left\lVert\mathbf{e}\right\rVert^{2}>\frac{\bar{d}^{2}}{\lambda_{\text{min}}(\mathbf{Q})\eta}$ . The tracking error is thus uniformly ultimately bounded by the sublevel set (28).∎

### -C A note on the diffeomorphic property of the learned transform

#### Exact feedback linearization.

As already established in Section III, the existence of an observable function $h(\mathbf{x})$ that satisfies conditions CA (or, equivalently, CB) generates a coordinate transformation $\Phi(\mathbf{x})$ that feedback linearizes the system by stacking the iterated Lie derivatives of $h$ . While conditions CA, together with successive time derivatives of $h(\mathbf{x})$ clearly demonstrate that the transformed dynamics form a chain of integrators, showing that $\Phi(\mathbf{x})$ constitutes a valid coordinate transformation requires establishing the nonsingularity of its Jacobian.

Following Lemma 4.1.1 in [9], consider the matrix-valued function $\mathbf{M}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ defined as

$$ \mathbf{M}=D_{\mathbf{x}}\Phi\,\begin{bmatrix}g&\mathrm{ad}_{f}g&\ldots&\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g\end{bmatrix}. $$

Under the standing assumptions for state feedback linearizability, the bracket matrix

$$ \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}g&\mathrm{ad}_{f}g&\ldots&\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g\end{bmatrix} $$

is nonsingular on $\mathcal{D}$ . Therefore, nonsingularity of $\mathbf{M}$ implies nonsingularity of $D_{\mathbf{x}}\Phi=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{G}^{-1}$ .

Invoking the basic algebraic properties of Lie brackets, $\mathbf{M}$ can be constructed column by column through the recursive relation (see Lemma 4.1.2 in [9])

$$ \mathbf{M}_{i,j+1}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\mathbf{M}_{i,j}-\mathbf{M}_{i+1,j},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1. $$

In addition, by construction of the feedback-linearizing coordinates,

$$ \phi_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{f}^{\,i-1}h, $$

and the relative-degree- $n$ condition gives

$$ \mathcal{L}_{g}h=\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}h=\cdots=\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{n-2}h=0,\qquad\beta:=\mathcal{L}_{g}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{n-1}h\neq 0. $$

Consequently, the first column of $\mathbf{M}$ is

$$ \mathbf{M}_{:,0}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&\ldots&0&\beta\end{bmatrix}^{\top}. $$

Propagating (36) through (33) yields the lower anti-triangular structure

$$ \mathbf{M}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0&\cdots&0&(-1)^{n-1}\beta\\
0&0&0&\cdots&(-1)^{n-2}\beta&*\\
0&0&0&\iddots&*&*\\
\vdots&\vdots&\iddots&\iddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&-\beta&*&\cdots&*&*\\
\beta&*&*&\cdots&*&*\end{bmatrix}. $$

The anti-diagonal entries are therefore nonzero whenever $\beta\neq 0$ , which is sufficient to establish the nonsingularity of $\mathbf{M}$ and, consequently, of $D_{\mathbf{x}}\Phi$ .

#### Approximate control conditions.

The previous argument relies on exact satisfaction of both the control conditions and the Lie-derivative cascade defining $\Phi$ . Nevertheless, the same construction provides a useful lens through which to understand how approximation errors affect the diffeomorphic property. We first consider the simpler case in which the Lie-derivative cascade remains exact, while the control conditions are satisfied only approximately. Let the learned coordinates be denoted by $\hat{\phi}_{i}$ , $i=1,\ldots,n$ , and assume

$$ \hat{\phi}_{i+1}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\phi}_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1. $$

The deviations from the control conditions can then be collected in the first column of $\hat{\mathbf{M}}$ by defining

$$ \epsilon_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{g}\hat{\phi}_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1,\qquad\epsilon_{n}=\mathcal{L}_{g}\hat{\phi}_{n}-\beta. $$

Consequently,

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}_{:,0}=\begin{bmatrix}\epsilon_{1}&\epsilon_{2}&\ldots&\epsilon_{n-1}&\beta+\epsilon_{n}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}. $$

Since the Lie-derivative cascade is still satisfied exactly, the same recursion as in the exact case holds,

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i,j+1}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i,j}-\hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i+1,j}. $$

Let $\Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}$ denote the component of the perturbation generated by the control residuals in the recursively determined portion of $\mathbf{M}$ . Its propagation is governed by

$$ \Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i,j+1}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i,j}-\Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i+1,j},\qquad\Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i,0}=\epsilon_{i}. $$

The first few propagated residuals are therefore

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i,1} \displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{f}\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{i+1}, \displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i,2} \displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{f}^{2}\epsilon_{i}-2\mathcal{L}_{f}\epsilon_{i+1}+\epsilon_{i+2}, $$

and, more generally,

$$ \Delta\mathbf{M}^{g}_{i,j}=\sum_{k=0}^{j}(-1)^{k}{j\choose k}\mathcal{L}_{f}^{\,j-k}\epsilon_{i+k},\qquad i+j\leq n. $$

Hence, the exact zero structure of $\mathbf{M}$ is no longer preserved: the control residuals appearing in the first column propagate toward the upper anti-triangular region and the anti-diagonal of $\mathbf{M}$ . Importantly, uniformly small values of $\epsilon_{i}$ do not directly imply a uniformly small perturbation of $\mathbf{M}$ , since the propagated entries depend on increasingly high Lie derivatives of the residual functions.

#### Approximate Lie-derivative consistency.

A second source of approximation arises when the learned coordinates do not satisfy the exact Lie-derivative structure, as is the case in our cascadic implementation. Define the corresponding consistency residuals as

$$ c_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\phi}_{i}-\hat{\phi}_{i+1},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1, $$

so that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\phi}_{i}=\hat{\phi}_{i+1}+c_{i}. $$

Letting

$$ V_{j}=\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{j}g, $$

the entries of the learned matrix are

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i,j}=\mathcal{L}_{V_{j}}\hat{\phi}_{i}. $$

Using $V_{j+1}=[f,V_{j}]$ and the commutator identity

$$ \mathcal{L}_{[f,V_{j}]}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\mathcal{L}_{V_{j}}-\mathcal{L}_{V_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{f}, $$

the recursive construction becomes

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i,j+1}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i,j}-\hat{\mathbf{M}}_{i+1,j}-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{j}g}c_{i}. $$

Thus, while the control residuals modify the initial condition of the recursion through the first column, the consistency residuals act as an additional forcing term injected at each stage of the recursive construction.

Subtracting the exact recursion (33) gives the perturbation dynamics

$$ \Delta\mathbf{M}_{i,j+1}=\mathcal{L}_{f}\Delta\mathbf{M}_{i,j}-\Delta\mathbf{M}_{i+1,j}-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{j}g}c_{i},\qquad\Delta\mathbf{M}_{i,0}=\epsilon_{i}. $$

Accordingly, the total perturbation can be interpreted as the superposition of a free response, generated by the control residuals $\epsilon_{i}$ through the initial condition, and a forced response, generated by the consistency residuals $c_{i}$ . Introducing the propagation operator

$$ (\mathcal{T}z)_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{f}z_{i}-z_{i+1}, $$

and the forcing

$$ (q_{j})_{i}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{j}g}c_{i}, $$

the perturbation in the $j$ -th column can be written compactly as

$$ \Delta\mathbf{M}_{j}=\mathcal{T}^{j}\epsilon-\sum_{s=0}^{j-1}\mathcal{T}^{\,j-1-s}q_{s}. $$

Due to the linearity of the recursive relation, this decomposition is directly analogous to the decomposition of a linear discrete system into its zero-input and zero-state responses. Both contributions involve derivatives of the learned residual functions and may therefore differ spatially from the residual values directly penalized during training. Importantly, however, the consistency contribution does not introduce an a priori higher differential order than the control contribution: at column $j$ , both involve derivatives of their respective residuals of order at most $j$ , with consistency errors introduced at later stages (which empirically appear larger) undergoing fewer subsequent propagation steps.

#### Structured perturbation and preservation of invertibility.

To study how the resulting perturbation affects invertibility, it is convenient to reverse the column ordering of $\mathbf{M}$ through a fixed permutation matrix $\mathbf{P}$ . The exact matrix

$$ \mathbf{L}^{\star}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{P} $$

is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal and is therefore invertible. The learned matrix can be decomposed as

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{L}^{\star}+\Delta\mathbf{L}+\mathbf{U}, $$

where $\Delta\mathbf{L}$ contains the perturbation in the strictly lower-triangular region, while $\mathbf{U}$ contains the complementary upper-triangular perturbation, including perturbations of the diagonal. This decomposition is applied to the total perturbation, independently of whether its entries originate from control or consistency errors.

Factoring out the exact matrix gives

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{L}^{\star}\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}\right), $$

where

$$ \mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{L}^{\star})^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{L},\qquad\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{L}^{\star})^{-1}\mathbf{U}. $$

Since $(\mathbf{L}^{\star})^{-1}$ is lower triangular and $\Delta\mathbf{L}$ is strictly lower triangular, $\mathbf{A}$ is itself strictly lower triangular and hence nilpotent,

$$ \mathbf{A}^{n}=0. $$

Consequently, $\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A}$ is always invertible and

$$ (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A})^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}\mathbf{A}^{k}. $$

In particular, perturbations confined to the strictly lower-triangular region cannot, by themselves, destroy invertibility.

Using (61), (58) can be factored further as

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{L}^{\star}(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A})\left(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{C}\right), $$

where

$$ \mathbf{C}:=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{B}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}\mathbf{A}^{k}\mathbf{B}. $$

Since the first two factors in (62) are invertible, preservation of invertibility reduces entirely to the last factor. In particular,

$$ \|\mathbf{C}\|_{2}<1 $$

is sufficient to guarantee that $\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{C}$ is invertible and, consequently, that $\hat{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{P}$ remains invertible.

The triangular structure provides a useful refinement of this condition. From (63),

$$ \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{B}+\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}\mathbf{A}^{k}\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{R}}, $$

where the interaction remainder $\mathbf{R}$ satisfies the exact bound

$$ \|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}^{k}\right)\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}. $$

Hence,

$$ \|\mathbf{C}\|_{2}\leq\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}^{k}\right)\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}, $$

and a sufficient condition for preservation of invertibility is therefore

$$ \boxed{\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}^{k}\right)\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}<1.} $$

The role of the triangular decomposition becomes particularly transparent by normalizing the perturbation with respect to the smallest singular value of the reference matrix. Let

$$ \mathbf{E}=\Delta\mathbf{L}+\mathbf{U}, $$

where $\Delta\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{U}$ denote, respectively, the strictly lower- and upper-triangular components of the perturbation. Since their supports are disjoint, they are orthogonal with respect to the Frobenius inner product, and thus

$$ \|\mathbf{E}\|_{F}^{2}=\|\Delta\mathbf{L}\|_{F}^{2}+\|\mathbf{U}\|_{F}^{2}. $$

In particular,

$$ \|\Delta\mathbf{L}\|_{F}\leq\|\mathbf{E}\|_{F},\qquad\|\mathbf{U}\|_{F}\leq\|\mathbf{E}\|_{F}. $$

Recalling

$$ \mathbf{A}=(\mathbf{L}^{\star})^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{L},\qquad\mathbf{B}=(\mathbf{L}^{\star})^{-1}\mathbf{U}, $$

and using

$$ \|(\mathbf{L}^{\star})^{-1}\|_{2}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{L}^{\star})},\qquad\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{X}\|_{F}, $$

we obtain

$$ \|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\|\Delta\mathbf{L}\|_{F}}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{L}^{\star})}\leq\eta,\qquad\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{U}\|_{F}}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{L}^{\star})}\leq\eta, $$

where we define the dimensionless perturbation level

$$ \boxed{\eta:=\frac{\|\mathbf{E}\|_{F}}{\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{L}^{\star})}.} $$

Consequently, for $\eta<1$ , the remainder term in (66) satisfies

$$ \|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{B}\|_{2}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2}^{k}\leq\eta\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\eta^{k}=\eta^{2}\frac{1-\eta^{\,n-1}}{1-\eta}. $$

Hence,

$$ \boxed{\|\mathbf{R}\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2})=\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\|\mathbf{E}\|_{F}^{2}}{\sigma_{\min}^{2}(\mathbf{L}^{\star})}\right).} $$

Thus,

$$ \mathbf{C}=\mathbf{B}+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{2}). $$

Therefore, the upper-triangular perturbation $\mathbf{U}$ constitutes the leading-order structure-breaking contribution, whereas the perturbation $\Delta\mathbf{L}$ in the lower-triangular region affects invertibility only through products with $\mathbf{U}$ , and hence only at second and higher orders.

Most importantly, whenever (68) is satisfied,

$$ \hat{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{P} $$

is invertible. Since $\mathbf{P}$ is a permutation matrix, this immediately implies that $\hat{\mathbf{M}}$ is invertible. Finally, under the standing feedback-linearizability assumption that

$$ \mathbf{G}=\begin{bmatrix}g&\mathrm{ad}_{f}g&\ldots&\mathrm{ad}_{f}^{n-1}g\end{bmatrix} $$

is nonsingular,

$$ D_{\mathbf{x}}\hat{\Phi}=\hat{\mathbf{M}}\mathbf{G}^{-1} $$

is also nonsingular. Hence, condition (68) provides a sufficient perturbation bound under which the learned transformation preserves the diffeomorphic property of the exact feedback-linearizing map.

### -D System synthesis details

As already described in Section VI-D, we synthesize exactly feedback linearizable systems via randomly generated diffeomorphisms building on a bidirectional affine coupling mechanism. After splitting the input $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}$ , the diffeomorphism is defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{y}_{1}=\mathbf{x}_{1}+t_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{2}) \displaystyle\mathbf{y}_{2}=\mathbf{x}_{2}+t_{2}(\mathbf{y}_{1}) $$

and $t_{1}$ , $t_{2}$ are parameterized as a linear combination of Gaussian kernel functions. In our experiments, we fix $s_{1}(\mathbf{x})=s_{2}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{1}$ and use Gaussian kernels to parameterize $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ . Analytically, we define each transformation as $t_{i}(\mathbf{x}):=\mathbf{W}_{i}\phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ , where $\mathbf{W}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(n/2)}$ is a weight matrix and $\phi_{i}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is a vector of Gaussian basis functions with components $\phi_{i,k}(\mathbf{x}):=\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_{i,k})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{i,k}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_{i,k})\right)$ for $k=1,\dots,d$ . Here, $\mathbf{c}_{i,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n/2}$ are the kernel centers and $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{i,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n/2)\times(n/2)}$ are diagonal covariance matrices. Thus, $t_{1}(\mathbf{x})$ and $t_{2}(\mathbf{x})$ are linear combinations of Gaussian kernels. We generate diverse invertible transforms by sampling the nonzero parameters of $t_{i}(\mathbf{x})$ uniformly.
